Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). As-Sulami read "ألم تر" with a sukun, which is jazm after jazm. It is reported from the author of al-Lawaamih that "ترأ" with an open hamza and a sukun on the ra' according to the original form, and this is the dialect of Taym. Al-Jumhur read "tarmihim" with a ta', and the bird is a collective noun in this reading, and his saying:

"Like birds that escape the driving storm with its hail."

It is also made masculine, as in the reading of Abu Hanifa, Ibn Ya'mar, Isa, and Talha in one narration from him: "yarmihim." It was also said the pronoun refers to "your Lord." Abraha fell ill and his fingers fell off one joint at a time, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart. Abu Maksum, his deputy, escaped, and a bird followed him until he reached the Negus and informed him of what had happened to the people; the bird struck him with its stone and he died before the king. The explanation of "sijjil" has preceded in Surah Hud, and "al-asf" in Surah al-Rahman. So it is as if it were said: you have known the deed of Allah your Lord with those who intended His sanctuary; He made their scheme go astray and destroyed them with the weakest of His armies, namely the birds, which by their nature do not kill.

The story of the elephant has been related by the people of biography (siyar) and exegesis, in long and short forms, and it may be consulted in their books. The companions of the elephant are Abraha ibn al-Sabbah al-Habashi and those of his soldiers who were with him. The apparent view is that it was one elephant, and this is the view of most. al-Dahhak said: eight elephants. It was also said: twelve elephants; and it was said: a thousand elephants. These are mutually contradictory statements. The army was sixty thousand, and none returned except their commander, with a small remnant. When they reported what they had seen, they perished. The elephant, when they directed it toward Mecca and it came near it, would kneel; and when they directed it toward Yemen or Syria, it would hasten. Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). As-Sulami read "ألم تر" with a sukun, which is jazm after jazm. It is reported from the author of al-Lawaamih that "ترأ" with an open hamza and a sukun on the ra' according to the original form, and this is the dialect of Taym. "Tara" is suspended (ta'liq), and the clause containing the interrogation is in a position of nasb governed by it; "kayfa" is an object of the verb. In His address to His Prophet (ﷺ) with His words "your Lord did", there is an honouring of him (ﷺ) and an elevation of his mention, as if He said: your Lord, your Worshipped One, is He who did that, not the idols of Quraysh, Isaf, Na'ila and others.

﴿Did He not make their scheme go astray﴾ and nullify it? It is said: "dalala kaydahum" when he made it lost and wasted; it was said of Imru' al-Qays: al-Dilleel, because he caused his father's kingdom to be lost, i.e., wasted it. The wasting of their scheme was that Allah the Exalted burned the house they had built, intending that the pilgrimage of the Arabs should turn to it; and that He destroyed them when they intended to demolish the House of Allah, the Ka'ba, by sending against them birds that came from the direction of the sea, being neither Najdi, nor Tihami, nor Hijazi, black, and it was said: green, the size of a swallow. Al-Jumhur read "tarmihim" with a ta', and the bird is a collective noun in this reading, and his saying:

"Like birds that escape the driving storm with its hail."

It is also made masculine, as in the reading of Abu Hanifa, Ibn Ya'mar, Isa, and Talha in one narration from him: "yarmihim." It was also said the pronoun refers to "your Lord." "With stones": each bird had a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, each stone above a lentil grain and below a chickpea, written on each stone was the name of its target; it would land on his head and exit from his backside. Abraha fell ill and his fingers fell off one joint at a time, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart. Abu Maksum, his deputy, escaped, and a bird followed him until he reached the Negus and informed him of what had happened to the people; the bird struck him with its stone and he died before the king. The explanation of "sijjil" has preceded in Surah Hud, and "al-asf" in Surah al-Rahman. They were likened to the stalk of the crop that was eaten, i.e., that the consumers fell upon it, which is that worms eat it, and to the chaff that animals ate and trampled. It is in accordance with the manners of the Qur'an, like His saying: ﴿they both used to eat food﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 75], or it is what had its grain eaten and remained empty, so it is ascribed to eating figuratively, since the thing eaten is its grain, not it. Al-Jumhur read "ma'kul" with a sukun on the hamza, which is the original, since the form is maf'ul from fa'ala. Abu al-Darda', as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, read it with a fatha on the hamza, following the vowel of the mim, which is anomalous; this is like their saying "mahmum" with a fatha on the ha' following the vowel of the mim. Ibn Ishaq said: when Allah turned the Abyssinians back from Mecca, the Arabs glorified the Quraysh and said: the People of Allah fought on their behalf and sufficed them the burden of their enemy. That was a blessing from Allah the Exalted upon them. It was also said: it was an answer to the supplication of the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him.
